sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Database normalization is the process of organizing a schema into tables and columns so that every fact is stored exactly once — eliminating **insertion, update, and deletion anomalies** — via a sequence of normal forms (1NF atomic, 2NF no partial dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency, BCNF) that trade read join cost for write integrity and storage minimality.

Normalization is the discipline of structuring a relational schema so that each fact lives in exactly one place. The motivation is anomaly elimination. Consider an unnormalized `orders` table with columns `(order_id, customer_name, customer_address, customer_email, items)` where `items` is a comma-separated list. Inserting a new order requires re-typing the customer's name/address/email (insertion anomaly); if a customer changes their email, you must update every row where they appear (update anomaly); if a customer's only order is deleted, you lose their name/address/email (deletion anomaly). Normalization fixes these by splitting into `customers(customer_id, name, address, email)` and `orders(order_id, customer_id, ...)` with a foreign key reference — the customer's name/email live in one row, referenced by all their orders. The trade-off is that queries now require **joins** to reassemble the denormalized view (`SELECT o.*, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id`), which costs I/O and CPU; this is why OLAP systems often denormalize intentionally (Topic 10). For OLTP systems, normalization is the default because write integrity dominates.

The normal forms build on each other. **1NF (First Normal Form)**: every column is atomic — no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists, no arrays. The `items` column above violates 1NF; fix by extracting into `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, price)`. **2NF (Second Normal Form)**: 1NF plus no partial dependency — every non-key column depends on the *whole* primary key, not part of it. In `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name)`, the `product_name` depends only on `product_id` (part of the composite key), not on `order_id`; this is a partial dependency. Fix by extracting `products(product_id, product_name)` and leaving `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity)`. **3NF (Third Normal Form)**: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key columns don't depend on other non-key columns. In `employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name, dept_location)`, `dept_name` and `dept_location` depend on `dept_id` (which is a non-key column), not on `emp_id` directly; this is transitive. Fix by extracting `departments(dept_id, dept_name, dept_location)` and leaving `employees(emp_id, dept_id)`. **BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)**: stricter 3NF — every determinant is a candidate key. BCNF catches cases 3NF misses (rare, involving overlapping candidate keys).

Real-world: Amazon's product catalog normalization. A naive schema would store product info with the seller and category info denormalized: `products(product_id, title, price, seller_name, seller_email, category_name, category_parent_name)`. This causes update anomalies (a seller changing their email requires updating millions of product rows) and storage bloat (the seller's email is duplicated across every product they sell). The normalized schema is: `products(product_id, title, price, seller_id, category_id)`, `sellers(seller_id, name, email, address)`, `categories(category_id, name, parent_category_id)`. Each fact lives once: the seller's email is in one row of `sellers`; updating it touches one row. The category hierarchy is a self-referencing table (`parent_category_id` foreign key to `categories`). Queries that need denormalized views (e.g., the product detail page showing seller name and category breadcrumb) join the three tables: `SELECT p.*, s.name, c.name, pc.name FROM products p JOIN sellers s ON p.seller_id=s.id JOIN categories c ON p.category_id=c.id JOIN categories pc ON c.parent_category_id=pc.id WHERE p.id=?`. The trade-off: every product detail page is a 4-table join, which costs ~10–20ms in PostgreSQL (with indexes on the FK columns). Amazon caches the denormalized result in a key-value store (DynamoDB) for sub-millisecond reads, refreshing the cache on writes — this is denormalization applied at the cache layer, with the database staying normalized for integrity.

The decision of "how far to normalize" depends on the workload. **OLTP workloads** (high writes, transactional integrity) normalize to 3NF or BCNF — write integrity is paramount, joins are acceptable because queries return few rows. **OLAP workloads** (analytics, dashboards, aggregations) often denormalize to a **star schema**: a central `fact_sales` table with foreign keys to `dim_product`, `dim_customer`, `dim_date`, `dim_store` dimension tables. The star schema is normalized in the sense that dimensions are separate tables, but denormalized in that dimensions are flat (no snowflaking of `dim_product` into `dim_category` and `dim_brand` — those columns live directly in `dim_product`). This balances join cost (analytics queries join fact to a few dimensions, not a deep snowflake) with storage (dimensions are small, fact is large). The fully-normalized "snowflake schema" (dimensions further normalized) is rarely used because the extra joins cost more than the storage savings. **Reporting workloads** often use a fully denormalized **materialized view** (Topic 10) for hot reports, with the underlying tables staying normalized for writes.

A practical note: normalization is a **write-optimization** that trades read cost. Every INSERT/UPDATE touches one row in one table (the customer's email update touches `customers` row only); a denormalized schema would touch many rows. But every read that needs the joined view pays the join cost. For read-heavy workloads, the join cost can dominate — which is why OLAP systems denormalize. For write-heavy workloads (financial transactions, inventory updates), normalization wins because write integrity and minimal write amplification matter most. The compromise pattern at scale: keep the **database normalized for integrity**, and add a **denormalized read model** (materialized view, cache, search index, or read replica with denormalized projections) for hot queries. Writes go to the normalized DB (one source of truth); reads go to the denormalized projection (refreshed via triggers, CDC, or scheduled jobs). This is the standard pattern at Netflix (normalized PostgreSQL for billing, denormalized Cassandra for viewing history), Amazon (normalized RDS for orders, denormalized DynamoDB for product catalog), and Uber (normalized MySQL for trip records, denormalized Redis for driver locations). The normalized DB is the system of record; the denormalized projections are performance optimizations.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD UN["Unnormalized:
orders(order_id, cust_name, cust_email, items_csv)"] --> Anomaly["Anomalies:
insert / update / delete"] UN --> NF1["1NF: atomic columns
extract items -> order_items(order_id, product_id, qty)"] NF1 --> NF2["2NF: no partial dep
extract product_name -> products(product_id, name)"] NF2 --> NF3["3NF: no transitive dep
extract dept_name -> departments(dept_id, name)"] NF3 --> BCNF["BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key"] BCNF --> Norm["Normalized schema:
integrity, minimal storage, write-friendly"] Norm -->|trade-off| Join["Reads require JOINs
slower for OLAP"] Join --> Denorm["Denormalize for read-heavy:
materialized view / cache / star schema"] Anomaly -->|fix| Norm ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` UNNORMALIZED (anomalies): +---------+----------+-------------+---------------------------+ | order_id| cust_name| cust_email | items | +---------+----------+-------------+---------------------------+ | 1 | Alice | alice@x.com | "book, pen, lamp" | | 2 | Alice | alice@x.com | "notebook" | <- cust duplicated | 3 | Bob | bob@y.com | "book" | +---------+----------+-------------+---------------------------+ Problems: - Insert: must retype Alice's email for every order (insertion anomaly) - Update: Alice changes email -> update rows 1 AND 2 (update anomaly) - Delete: delete order 3 -> lose Bob's name/email (deletion anomaly) - items_csv violates 1NF (not atomic) NORMALIZED (3NF): customers(id, name, email) -- Alice, Bob live here once orders(id, customer_id -> customers.id) -- foreign key reference order_items(order_id -> orders.id, product_id -> products.id, qty) products(id, name, price) -- product_name lives here once Each fact stored once. Anomalies gone. Trade-off: SELECT o.*, c.name, oi.qty, p.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON ... JOIN order_items oi ON ... JOIN products p ON ... -> 4-table JOIN to reassemble the denormalized view ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Normalization eliminates insertion, update, and deletion anomalies by ensuring each fact lives in exactly one row of one table. The cost is that reads requiring the joined view must JOIN multiple tables — slower I/O and CPU. 2. The normal forms cascade: 1NF (atomic columns, no repeating groups), 2NF (no partial dependency on part of a composite key), 3NF (no transitive dependency on a non-key column), BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Each form removes a specific class of anomaly. 3. The normalized schema is the system of record (write integrity, minimal storage). For read-heavy workloads, add denormalized projections (materialized views, caches, star schemas) — writes go to the normalized DB, reads go to the denormalized projection refreshed via triggers, CDC, or scheduled jobs. This is the standard pattern at Netflix, Amazon, and Uber.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Database normalization demo with sqlite3.
- CREATE TABLE orders_unnormalized ( order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, cust_name TEXT, cust_email TEXT, items TEXT -- comma-separated "product_name:qty" );
- CREATE TABLE customers ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, email TEXT NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE products ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,…
- SELECT o.id, c.name, c.email, p.name, oi.quantity, oi.unit_price_cents FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON…
- Update anomaly: Alice changes email; must update ALL her rows
- Insert each fact once
- Update anomaly: GONE in normalized
- Reassemble the denormalized view via JOIN

```python
"""
Database normalization demo with sqlite3.

Demonstrates:
  1. Unnormalized table (anomalies)
  2. 1NF: extract items -> order_items
  3. 2NF: extract product_name -> products
  4. 3NF: extract customer info -> customers (separate from orders)
  5. Compare INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE behavior
  6. Show the JOIN needed to reassemble the denormalized view

Run:  python3 normalization_demo.py
"""

import sqlite3, tempfile, os

path = tempfile.mktemp(suffix=".db")
conn = sqlite3.connect(path)
cur  = conn.cursor()

# --- UNNORMALIZED schema ---
cur.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders_unnormalized (
    order_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    cust_name   TEXT,
    cust_email  TEXT,
    items       TEXT        -- comma-separated "product_name:qty"
);
""")

cur.executemany("INSERT INTO orders_unnormalized VALUES (?,?,?,?)", [
    (1, "Alice", "alice@x.com", "Book:1,Pen:2,Lamp:1"),
    (2, "Alice", "alice@x.com", "Notebook:3"),
    (3, "Bob",   "bob@y.com",   "Book:1"),
])
conn.commit()
print("== Unnormalized (anomalies) ==")
print("  orders_unnormalized:")
for r in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM orders_unnormalized ORDER BY order_id"):
    print(f"    {r}")

# --- Update anomaly: Alice changes email; must update ALL her rows ---
print("\n  UPDATE anomaly: Alice changes email to alice@new.com")
print("  -> must update rows 1 AND 2 (Alice appears twice)")
cur.execute("UPDATE orders_unnormalized SET cust_email='alice@new.com' WHERE cust_name='Alice'")
print("  rows updated:", cur.rowcount)
conn.commit()

# --- NORMALIZED 3NF schema ---
cur.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    email TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE products (
    id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
    created_at   INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
    product_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
    quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL        -- snapshot at order time
);
""")

# insert each fact once
cur.execute("INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Alice', 'alice@x.com')")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Bob', 'bob@y.com')")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price_cents) VALUES ('Book', 1200)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price_cents) VALUES ('Pen', 150)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price_cents) VALUES ('Lamp', 2500)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price_cents) VALUES ('Notebook', 400)")

alice_id = cur.execute("SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name='Alice'").fetchone()[0]
bob_id   = cur.execute("SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name='Bob'").fetchone()[0]

book_id    = cur.execute("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name='Book'").fetchone()[0]
pen_id     = cur.execute("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name='Pen'").fetchone()[0]
lamp_id    = cur.execute("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name='Lamp'").fetchone()[0]
notebook_id= cur.execute("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name='Notebook'").fetchone()[0]

cur.execute("INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, created_at) VALUES (?, 1000)", (alice_id,))
o1 = cur.lastrowid
cur.execute("INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, created_at) VALUES (?, 1001)", (alice_id,))
o2 = cur.lastrowid
cur.execute("INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, created_at) VALUES (?, 1002)", (bob_id,))
o3 = cur.lastrowid

cur.executemany("INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents) VALUES (?,?,?,?)", [
    (o1, book_id, 1, 1200), (o1, pen_id, 2, 150), (o1, lamp_id, 1, 2500),
    (o2, notebook_id, 3, 400),
    (o3, book_id, 1, 1200),
])
conn.commit()

print("\n== Normalized 3NF (each fact once) ==")
print("  customers:")
for r in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM customers"): print(f"    {r}")
print("  products:")
for r in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM products"): print(f"    {r}")
print("  orders:")
for r in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM orders"): print(f"    {r}")
print("  order_items:")
for r in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM order_items"): print(f"    {r}")

# --- Update anomaly: GONE in normalized ---
print("\n  UPDATE fix: Alice changes email to alice@new.com")
print("  -> update ONE row in customers only")
cur.execute("UPDATE customers SET email='alice@new.com' WHERE name='Alice'")
print("  rows updated:", cur.rowcount)

# --- Reassemble the denormalized view via JOIN ---
print("\n  Denormalized view (re-assembled via JOIN):")
for r in cur.execute("""
    SELECT o.id, c.name, c.email, p.name, oi.quantity, oi.unit_price_cents
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
    ORDER BY o.id, p.name
"""):
    print(f"    order={r[0]} cust={r[1]} email={r[2]} prod={r[3]} qty={r[4]} price={r[5]}")

# --- Deletion anomaly: GONE ---
print("\n  DELETE fix: delete Bob's order; Bob's customer record is preserved")
cur.execute("DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ?", (o3,))
cur.execute("DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = ?", (o3,))
print("  Bob still in customers:", cur.execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name='Bob'").fetchone())

conn.close()
os.unlink(path)
```

quiz.question: What is 1NF, and how do you detect violations?
options: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is a stricter version of 3NF: every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y must have X as a superkey (i.e., X uniquely determines a row).
The violation is a transitive dependency: dept_name and dept_location depend on dept_id (a non-key column), not directly on emp_id.
The entities and their relationships: artists have albums; albums have tracks; users have playlists; playlists contain tracks (with an order).
First Normal Form (1NF) requires that every column holds atomic values — no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists, no arrays, no nested tables.
quiz.explanation: First Normal Form (1NF) requires that every column holds atomic values — no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists, no arrays, no nested tables. Each row-column intersection is a single value. Violations: (1) comma-separated lists — orders.items = "Book:1,Pen:2,Lamp:1" is one cell holding multiple facts; you can't query "which orders contain a Book" without parsing the string.

quiz.question: What is 2NF, and how does it differ from 3NF?
options: star schema** is the standard schema for OLAP/data warehouses: a central fact table (e.g., fact_sales) containing measures (numeric values to aggregate, like revenue, units_sold) and…
Normalization optimizes for write integrity and storage minimality at the cost of read join cost.
BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is a stricter version of 3NF: every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y must have X as a superkey (i.e., X uniquely determines a row).
The difference: 2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key; 3NF is about transitive dependencies through non-key columns.
quiz.explanation: 2NF (Second Normal Form): 1NF plus no partial dependency — every non-key column must depend on the whole primary key, not part of it. This only applies to tables with composite primary keys. Example: order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name) with PK (order_id, product_id).

quiz.question: What is BCNF, and when does it differ from 3NF?
options: The difference: 2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key; 3NF is about transitive dependencies through non-key columns.
star schema** is the standard schema for OLAP/data warehouses: a central fact table (e.g., fact_sales) containing measures (numeric values to aggregate, like revenue, units_sold) and…
Normalization optimizes for write integrity and storage minimality at the cost of read join cost.
BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is a stricter version of 3NF: every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y must have X as a superkey (i.e., X uniquely determines a row).
quiz.explanation: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is a stricter version of 3NF: every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y must have X as a superkey (i.e., X uniquely determines a row). 3NF allows a non-key column to be a determinant if it's a candidate key, but BCNF doesn't. BCNF differs from 3NF only when a table has overlapping candidate keys (multiple composite candidate keys sharing columns).

quiz.question: What is the trade-off between normalization and denormalization?
options: star schema** is the standard schema for OLAP/data warehouses: a central fact table (e.g., fact_sales) containing measures (numeric values to aggregate, like revenue, units_sold) and…
The difference: 2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key; 3NF is about transitive dependencies through non-key columns.
BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is a stricter version of 3NF: every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y must have X as a superkey (i.e., X uniquely determines a row).
Normalization optimizes for write integrity and storage minimality at the cost of read join cost.
quiz.explanation: Normalization optimizes for write integrity and storage minimality at the cost of read join cost. Denormalization optimizes for read performance at the cost of write amplification and storage bloat, plus the risk of inconsistency if updates miss some copies. Normalized: each fact lives in one row; updates touch one row (no anomalies); reads require JOINs to reassemble the denormalized view (slower I/O, more CPU).

quiz.question: When should you use a surrogate key vs a natural key?
options: The denormalized customer_email in orders is a classic read-optimization-vs-write-integrity trade-off.
Composite natural key (tenant_id, user_id): pros — no extra column, business-meaningful (queries always filter by tenant), enforces uniqueness per tenant naturally.
The entities and their relationships: artists have albums; albums have tracks; users have playlists; playlists contain tracks (with an order).
natural key** is a column (or set of columns) with business meaning that uniquely identifies a row — e.g., users(email), products(sku), countries(iso_code).
quiz.explanation: natural key** is a column (or set of columns) with business meaning that uniquely identifies a row — e.g., users(email), products(sku), countries(iso_code). A surrogate key is an artificial identifier with no business meaning — e.g., users(id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT), products(id UUID).
